utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber understand that there are a few procedural matters which we'll deal with later this morning. They're not of such an urgency that we could not yet start with the witness. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: DAVORIN PAVLOVIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I'd like to remind you that the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony is still binding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please approach the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please come closer to the microphone, Mr. Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, you can for now keep the binder closed and put the statement away. If I need to refer you to that, I will let you know. We left off yesterday talking about Donji Lapac, and as the Presiding Judge correctly pointed out, it would be now being west of Donji Lapac on the map. As you were in Boricevac which is outside of Donji Lapac right on the state border, across from Kulen Vakuf, how long did you stay in Boricevac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Counsel, on that day I stayed very briefly, just an hour to an hour and a half, and then I went back to Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could please call up D555.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Pavlovic, you can please open your binder to tab 15. And in the English version it's page 47 of 65. And on the Croatian version you'll see on the left-hand side --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you go to the next page, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: You'll see in the Croatian version it's entry 332, which would be the same entry on the Croatian version. I don't have that currently in front of me. Mr. Pavlovic -- Mr. Pavlovic, can you tell us what page you're on, if there's a page designation on the bottom of your document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't see. It says D00555 at the bottom, but I can't see what the page is. I'm sorry, it says 95, but it's hardly legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That would be the Croatian page number 95 then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And if you'll see on the left-hand column of this document there are entries in numerical order. For example in the English version it starts at 327 and goes to 334.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's it. Thank you, Mr. Registrar, for finding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, there's an entry there, 332, at 2120 hours, and that's an August 7th entry, 1995. The entry reads: "Mr. Markac (D. Lapac) reports that from the north direction one unit with which he has no contact is closing in on him. ZP Gosic /illegible/ was informed about this, but they haven't gotten anything to do with such unit in the north. General Markac was tasked to establish contact all by himself." Now, Mr. Pavlovic, are you familiar with this -- with what this reference refers to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Chamber what that is in reference to and from where this report came from, the location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was like this: Upon our return to Gracac, we received information about the further actions of the army or unknown units towards Lapac, and General Markac from Gracac rang up the Main Staff on the phone, because that was the only point where we did have a telephone, and he established contact through an encrypted telephone line with the Main Staff, and in my opinion he protested. I think he talked to General Miljavac. He had a rather heated conversation with him and said that unknown units were coming in from the direction Udbina and that he assumed that it was the 9th Guards Brigade which was in the Gospic military district, and he asked that communication be established with that unit as soon as possible and that all artillery attack on Lapac be stopped immediately, and in the meantime we received information that some houses had been targeted already, so he wanted to stop the firing and destruction of property in Lapac. I saw that General Markac was rather upset and this was unusual for him. He started shouting and asked them to stop the artillery attack and fire in that part of Lapac immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, would it have been possible for General Markac to contact the Main Staff from Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he couldn't do that either from Boricevac or from Donji Lapac or from anywhere else. The only point where we could make contact was at Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, after the conclusion of Operation Storm in terms of the role of the Special Police, there was a withdrawal to -- you were ordered to go to Petrova Gora.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Counsel, as far as I remember, on the 8th in Boricevac, we had a meeting of commanders, and part of the units -- or part of the units were ordered to return to base. The other units on the following day received orders to return. In the meantime, we received information that we would be going to Petrova Gora, and I ordered some communications men to prepare for that and pull out of the area and move towards Vojnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, if you could please open to tab 29 of your book. That is D557. In terms of the former -- former Sectors North and South, where was Petrova Gora located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Petrova Gora was located in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sector North. Interpreter's correction, Sector North.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll see, Mr. Pavlovic, this is an order dated the 10th of August, 1995, from the Main Staff asking or ordering General Markac to engage in mop-up operations in Petrova Gora. You were a participant in that; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How long of a time period were the Special Police in Petrova Gora?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in Petrova Gora -- well, I think we were there for a couple of days. Four days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And then where did the units go after Petrova Gora -- the Petrova Gora operation was completed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that, Counsel, we returned to base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: What base was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Each to his own unit. We returned to the Ministry of the Interior where the Special Police Sector base was and as was my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Other than the staff office that was maintained in Gracac, could you please tell the Chamber whether or not there were any Special Police operations conducted in Sector South from August 9th to August 21st of 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the disposal of the Gracac staff there was always a unit numbering 30 men, and they rotated, and that was under the police group of Gospic and another one, and they gathered different information, what was going on in the field, where there had been contact with the enemy, and they informed the Special Police Sector about activities of that kind, and at the same time the sector gathered information from the police administrations in the area, three police administrations, in fact. One was Zadar, one was Gospic, and the other was in Split. So information and data was gathered there about contacts and straggler enemy soldiers and sabotage groups, terrorist groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber, please, was it your experience both in the areas where the Special Police were in operation during Operation Storm and in other areas -- as soon as an area was liberated, could you explain to the Trial Chamber who came in behind the Special Police and any other military force that would have been in Sector South to establish law and order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've already said that already on the second day of the operation we opened police stations in Lovinac and Gracac, and the police stations, once the special units had passed by, were established in Donji and Gornji Lapac as well, and later on, according to their plan, they opened some more police stations and border police posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: So as far as civil control of the area, that was passed on to the civil police and the civil authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's what the order was. The role of the Special Police in this operation was to suppress the enemy forces and to advance speedily, and then the regular police entered afterwards and took over the role that they were entitled to take by law, ensuring law and order, preventing crime, issuance of documents, and everything else that the regular police force does generally.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all unnecessary microphones be switched off in the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I will make sure I turn my mike off after I speak. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, I would like you to please go to -- you don't have this document in your booklet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: P1237, please, if that could be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: And while the document is brought up on the screen, Mr. Pavlovic, I'll just preview the subject matter of this set of questions. This deals with the issue of check-points and whether or not the Special Police was involved in check-points. We have in this particular document, P1273 -- the English version is page 3, and the Croatian version, I think it's on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: One more page in the Croatian version, please. There we go. In the middle of the Croatian version where it says "Zapovjedniku." And in the English version if you could highlight the section that says "We entered the suburb of Gracac."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, are you familiar -- in the middle of that paragraph in Croatian where it says "Zapovjedniku," there's a sentence and I'll read it in English: "We entered the suburbs of Gracac, namely the village of Loncari, at 1400 hours on 5 August. BPP, barrier check-points, were put in that village, and we replenished the MTS, materiel and technical equipment." Could you please explain to the Trial Chamber what BPP means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: BPP is combat barrier check-points which were always established at the flank of a unit in order to ensure that we're not surprised by a counter-attack by the enemy forces or some other sabotage or terrorist group, and these barriers or check-points are erected while the unit is in the area. As soon as the unit moves on, the -- this barrier check-point is moved and follows the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pavlovic. I'd like to move, please, to D561, which is tab 37. Mr. Pavlovic, D561 is an August 21 order regarding the conduct of mop-up operations. Are you familiar with the order and the issues surrounding this order from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Counsel. I am aware of this document. I was informed of it by General Markac who called us to come to the sector and acquainted us with the contents of this document. Let me explain. I was the assistant commander in the Main Staff of the Special Police, and I didn't actually see the document, but General Markac or Mr. Sacic informed us of its contents and we acted upon it, whether organising communications or organising people to go out into an operation or whatever. As far as I remember, General Markac called us and said that he had received an order of this kind and that he had talked over the phone with the Main Staff. I think it was with General Cervenko, who told him orally that we were to return to the area -- to the south for the mopping up operation, search and mop-up. The terminology is search and mopping up. Well, it's the same term. It's the same concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly explain, Mr. Pavlovic, what the Special Police did and what the purpose was of the mop-up and search operations in -- after August 21st of 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Counsel, the search of the terrain in a certain area -- well, what we did was to deploy the special forces, and they were given the task of uncovering stragglers, armed enemy soldiers, sabotage and terrorist groups, mines and other technical devices, minefields, depots and hidden weapons or hidden enemy soldiers such as in various caves or trenches, and we had to search the waterways as well to see that they hadn't left any weapons in ponds, rivers, et cetera, waterways.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, in paragraphs 21 and 22 of your statement, if you could please refer to those as I ask you these questions. That's D1830. You talk generally about the communication between the headquarters and axis commanders -- axis commanders and communications between commanders for various units. In the second sentence of paragraph 21: "At the staff and at the IZM --" If you can -- do you have your statement there, Mr. Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "At the staff and at the IZM it was not possible to monitor the communication between the axis commanders and the subgroup commanders and personnel, members of the Special Police Units on the ground, while combat tasks were being carried out." And then paragraph 22, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you could scroll down on the Croatian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The last sentence says: "This way of establishing and using the communications system was also implemented at the end of Operation Storm during the search of some ground in the newly liberated with the aim of finding straggling terrorists when the SJP joint forces were appointed for these tasks." What I wanted to ask you, Mr. Pavlovic, regarding these two portions of your statement, is during mop-up operations was it possible for the units engaged in mop-up operations to communicate via radio or any other means of communication with the staff in Gracac, and if not or if yes, please explain how or why.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Counsel, every time the unit went out into the field a mobile repeater station put up in a heavy-duty vehicle went with it to enable communication for that narrow area, because it was impossible to ensure communication between the Main Staff in Gracac and these so-called forward command posts, because the distance was greater and given the configuration of the terrain. Now, as they moved to a different area every day, it wasn't possible to ensure communication and so the commanders -- or, rather, the commander who conducted the search was in a certain locality with his unit and was able to contact the unit throughout the operation, but when he came back to the Main Staff and headquarters in the evening, he would report orally and in writing. Sometimes it was an oral report. Sometimes he would write a written report which he would hand over to Mr. Markac or Mr. Sacic at headquarters in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Pavlovic. In we could please move to D739. Just tab 39 in your book, Mr. Pavlovic. This set of question -- questions relates to the freedom train operation in which the Special Police participated on August 26th. D739 is an order or is a document dated August 23rd, 1995, and on the second page of the English -- and I think we can go to the second page of the Croatian as well, please. There's a notation there that the: "ATJ MUP in coordination with the chief of operation administration of GSHV, which is the Main Staff of the Croatian military, Major General Vinko Vrbanac, will take over security of the most delicate part of the railroad." Mr. Pavlovic, were you involved with this operation regarding the freedom train?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Counsel, as far as I remember, we were not involved nor were we charged with communicating the route for the members of the ATJ. With some members of the staff I was at the railway when the train was supposed to pass there, but we had a different task, and I simply happened to find myself there, but I did not take part in securing the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The Special Police, however, was involved in securing a portion of that path; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could look at D563, which is tab 41 of your book. And in the English version we can go to page 4, please. Just for reference, this is an August 25, 1995, letter from the national security office staff. If we could go to page 4 of the Croatian, please. The paragraph under RH Ministry of the Interior has a discussion, and I'll read the section here: "After the meeting of the security staff, the Knin 95 OA Staff was formed at the level of RH MUP with Deputy Minister Zlatko Gledec at its head and Smiljan Reljic, Josko Moric, Mladen Markac, Igor Bozikovic, Stjepan Klasic, and the chief of the police department, Andjelko Sacic, as members. Now, were you aware General Markac's participation in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Counsel, I do not remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: But you do know that General Markac was involved in planning for security of the freedom train; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Counsel, as far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could please pull up tab D564, which is for you, Mr. Pavlovic, tab 43. D564 is a letter dated September 1st of 1995, and it's from General Norac to the Main Staff, which requests in paragraph 2 -- or in paragraph 4 -- it's the second page of the English, and I believe it's also the second page of the Croatian. The letter in general describes operations in the Gospic military district in terms of remaining enemy soldiers, among other things, and in paragraph 4 General Norac writes to the Main Staff: "Since we did not conduct a detailed search in the area of responsibility of the Military District Gospic, we assume that the possible outlaw groups could be in the wider area of Plitvice Lakes ..." and it describes where, "... and we believe it is necessary to employ special MUP troops to conduct searches of that area." Now, Mr. Pavlovic, were you -- did the Special Police then conduct these operations in Plitvice Lakes? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel. In early September, I think it was around the 6th of September, we sent the staff to Plitvice, and we also moved a part of the special units to that area, and for several days, according to certain plans, we conducted the search of the terrain, and I think that we stayed there until around the 12th of September. I remember that General Markac and myself and several other members of the staff, while passing through Plitvice, and going to certain places, we even came across minefields which we managed to skirt at the very last moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: How long of a period of time -- oh, you -- I'm sorry, you said that. You were there until September 12th. After -- and Plitvice is located in Sector North?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Counsel, I'm really not sure where Plitvice is located, but it's at a point somewhere in the middle or between Sectors South and Sector North. It is on the main road between Gracac and Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when did the Special Police end mop-up operations in Sector South?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Counsel, I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Chamber when, as far as you're aware, the Special Police concluded mop-up operations in Sector South, the joint forces of the Special Police with which you were working.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Counsel, in early October, around the 9th or the 10th of October, we concluded the operation of searching the terrain in Sector South and returned to our base. Further searches were conducted by police administrations on the basis of the information they had, and they had at their disposal their own special units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, I wanted to ask you generally regarding Mr. Markac's mindset when you were around him. Can you tell us, please, what his sentiments were in dealing with non-Croats that he would encounter during the course of his work with you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President; good morning, Your Honours. Perhaps it would be most straight forward to ask what Mr. Markac said rather than what his mindset was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I took it that Mr. Kuzmanovic was inquiring without saying whether it was words or written document, whatever information the witness has which would for him be indicative for the mindset of Mr. Markac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I guess I could be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If you could please describe for the Trial Chamber the nature and level of his character and professionalism and his conduct toward others, whatever their ethnic group was, while you were in his presence and working with him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had the honour since the beginning of the war and throughout the war to be together with General Markac. I came to know him quite well. He's a highly moral person, without any prejudice. He's a very socially sensitive person who took equal care of the special units and other members of the Ministry of the Interior, as well as of the civilians we came across in the occupied territory whom he always tried to take care of. Several times I had the opportunity to see when he ordered Mr. Bolje [phoen] to provide water, food, and cigarettes to them, and cigarettes were something that was highly estimated in the area. On several occasions I was in direct conflict with General Markac when he sent units of greater force than necessary to pull out our wounded, because if we received any information on a wounded or killed member of the Special Police, he did everything he could to provide assistance to such members as soon as possible. And once we were this conflict because he sent a helicopter deep into enemy territory where we had a wounded member. I explained to him that we could lose the helicopter. However, insisted that a helicopter be sent there anyway because this member of the special forces had been shot in the belly and his intestines were spilling out and so on. So we did send a helicopter. The helicopter was shot by enemy soldiers, but it managed to pull out this wounded man, but as a consequence we were left without the helicopter for a month, and we had to supply our men on Velebit on horseback or on foot rather than by helicopter. So he is a man who even shed tears on several occasions when he met mothers of his co-soldiers who had been killed. As I said, he was a highly moral person. He honoured all laws, General Markac did. He and myself had spent is a lot of time in the police before the war. We were used to the moral code, to respect the laws of the former republic of Croatia, which was a part of the former Yugoslavia, as well as the laws of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war began, General Markac was a -- involved with the police; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I know, he was working in the police administration in Zagreb. He was the former Secretariat of the Interior ministry for Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Chamber what discussions, warnings, or instructions were given with regard to the treatment of combatants, enemy combatants, by General Markac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, General Markac and Mr. Sacic always briefed us about the area where we had to operate, how we would do that, who would take part in the operations. Combat operations and tasks were always described. There were never political speeches given or anything of the kind. Honouring international conventions, treaties, and the laws of the Republic of Croatia was always stressed. Yesterday, I already said that we had orders that in case of taking prisoner of enemy soldiers we should disarm such persons, search them, and call on the regular police to take over them. And as for civilians, our duty was to take care of them, give them water, and also call on the regular police which would then call the civilian protection, which would protect the civilians. And the orders that we received at meetings I would forward to my own personnel in the Communications Unit so that they would know how to conduct themselves in such situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, I don't have any further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Very briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will now be cross-examined, Mr. Pavlovic, by Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pavlovic. I just want to clarify one issue with you. When you were talking about moving into the Donji Lapac area that you reference at paragraph 17 of your statement, D1830, and also talk about in the order of D552, am I correct in saying that when you were talking about moving into Donji Lapac and being in Donji Lapac there was no troops from the Split Military District in the Donji Lapac area? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Counsel. Yes, that is correct, because we did not see any soldiers from the Split Military District at all but, rather, as I was entering Lapac I heard on the radio communication that they had linked up in Otric with the soldiers from the Split Military District, and I didn't see them in Lapac on that day or on the next day in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, are you ready to cross-examine Mr. Pavlovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Waespi. Mr. Waespi is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pavlovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about the person who -- the persons who interviewed you during the interview process with the Defence of Mr. Markac. Can you look at the front page of your witness statement, which is D1830. We see that you're interviewed by Djurica Franjo and Anto Soljic. Now, let me first ask about Mr. Djurica Franjo. Did you know him at the time you met with him for the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I have known Mr. Djurica Franjo for a long time. He was the chief of the police sector, and he was my colleague as I was the chief of the operative equipment sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you meet with him during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Prosecutor. As my sector was responsible for the communications system of the Special Police, my sector was also responsible for the communications system of the regular police and Criminal Investigation Police. So we were always together with whoever was on the ground. And as the regular police followed Special Police, some of the communications personnel established communications systems for the duty operations of regular police as was possible on the ground, and I coordinated these activities with Mr. Moric and Mr. Franjo Djurica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in relation to Mr. Anto Soljic, I think yesterday you mentioned his name, that at one time you went with him on foot onto the forward command post during Operation Storm or just before Operation Storm was launched.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Prosecutor. Mr. Soljic as the chief of the internal control department, together with Mr. Djurica and myself, on the night before the operation, on the 3rd of August at night, we came to the forward command post Veliki Golic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Since when did you know that these two gentlemen were working as investigators or interviewers for the Markac Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly in terms of time, but I know that from the moment when the Defence team of General Markac was constituted I learned that three of my colleagues were there. One was Mr. Soljic. Another was Mr. Djurica, and the third one was Mr. Kranj [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was Mr. Kranj's role during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I said Mr. Kralj. I did not see them in the area, and I do not know anything about his role during the Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pavlovic. Let me move on to your function during Operation Storm. Now, I understand that you were the chief of Operative Equipment Sector. That's, I think, what I picked up from your witness statement. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Prosecutor. It was the Operative Equipment Sector. It included communications, telecommunications, transport, technology, cryptographic data protection, vehicles including special equipment for police and Special Police, and including weapons and technical protection means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In 1995 did you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the Chief Inspector of the interior ministry, and that was the highest rank that a policeman can have in the interior ministry, and I received it by a decree of the President Franjo Tudjman. I was given the rank of reserve colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that there were 60 people under your command during Operation Storm or working for you, and you explained there were mostly Croats, but there were also Serbs and others ethnicities. Were there officers and NCOs or just soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, employees of the Operative Equipment Sector were employees of the interior ministry who had certain titles of the interior ministry, so they did not have any military ranks, but they had police ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But were they structured in a certain sense or were you in command of all the 60 people together or was there an intermediate level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, there were several levels. I had an assistant for communications. That was Mr. Bradovski who was the communications chief in my sector. Below him he had the heads of departments. We had three departments in the structure. We had the department of radio communications, the department of communications, and the department shortwave communications, and each department had its own commander so that I did not directly command everyone, but I had to transfer the command to the chief of communications and then he would forward it to these three heads of departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. To whom did you report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, for the Special Police affairs, I was responsible to General Markac. For the regular police business I was responsible to Mr. Moric. I personally, as sector head, was responsible to the Deputy Minister of the Interior, Mr. Gledec, according to hierarchy, as I did not have an assistant minister above me, then I was directly responsible to the deputy or, rather, to the minister of the interior himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 5 of your witness statement you describe various members of the command staff of General Markac, and you mention, for instance, Mr. Sacic, the Chief of Operations, you mention the assistant commander for intelligence. What was his name, the assistant commander of intelligence that worked under General Markac at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, that was the chief of internal control, Mr. Soljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then the commander of the reserve force, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the reserve control was led by Mr. Maduna, and he co-operated with the department for -- the reserve force the Ministry of the Interior because the Special Police reserve force could only be called up by the reserve department of the Ministry of the Interior, Mr. Maduna coordinated all that. Now, whether there was anyone else except Mr. Maduna, I really can't remember just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You mentioned a liaison officer for the HV. Do you remember the name of that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The name of the artillery commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was Mr. Turkalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And were you as chief of Operative Equipment Sector also part of that command staff of General Markac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very briefly, how were you organised? How was the command staff of General Markac organised? Did you meet regularly before Operation Storm and during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in principle I learnt about individual tasks and assignments before the other commanders were called to the headquarters to be briefed because I had to plan the communications system, which was a rather complex one. So I had the opportunity of meeting with Mr. Markac and Mr. Sacic before the operation and planned together with them. They planned their forces. I planned the communications system, and then we linked up, compiled documentation and so on and so forth, and after that all the commanders would have a meeting all together at headquarters where either General Markac or Mr. Sacic would inform all of us of the details of the operation itself, how it would take place, which commanders and which units would take what directions and axis and who would be the commander of each individual axis or the individual groups and subgroups.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: After Operation Storm has commenced, was there a similar meeting or series of meetings when General Markac would call all the members of his command staff together and discuss where you were at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I said yesterday that on the 31st of July we had a meeting of commanders in Stari Grad, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- near --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sorry to cut you off. I'm interested in after the Operation Storm started. So on the 5th of August, 6th of August, 7th of August, did you have a joint meeting again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did, Mr. Prosecutor. We did have meetings of that kind, and they would be in the evening at the headquarters in Gracac where we were -- there would be a briefing, a short briefing telling us what happened that day and our assignments for the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pavlovic. Let me go on to something you mentioned today but also yesterday about the issue of how to treat civilians, and I quote you from yesterday at page 25248. You said, when asked about instructions you received: "If we encountered civilians, those civilians had to be sent to the basic police force. They were to report to the police in order to ensure their documents and accommodation, food, and water." Was that an instruction you had received from Mr. Sacic on the 31st July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move to the Gracac headquarter. I think you testified yesterday that it was the -- located at the municipal building in -- in Gracac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. It was in the Municipal Court building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Now, from when to when was it operational?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The staff in Gracac was established on the 5th in the afternoon, the 5th of August, that is, in the afternoon, and it was in that location until the beginning of October. I think it was until the 9th or 10th of October of that same year, unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how was it staffed? How many people worked there? And if it changed over time, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning there were a lot of people in the facility. There were the communications employees until the communications system had been set up properly. Then there was General Markac, Mr. Sacic, the internal control people led by Mr. Soljic. I was there. So quite a lot of people. And later on, after the operation, that is to say sometime around the 9th, we were there. There was always a duty officer 'round the clock. And at the beginning, in the first month or so, there was also a communications man for maintenance or maintaining the communications system generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You also said, I think in your witness statement, paragraph 12, that once the Gracac headquarter was established that the previous two command posts in Seline and on Mount Velebit were dissolved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the Veliki Golic forward command post was dissolved straight away. Now, I don't remember whether the same thing happened with the headquarters in Seline, whether it was on that day or another day, but I do know that the members of the staff relocated to Gracac the next day at around noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I think we have seen a document which is now D1831 which you have been shown yesterday, dated 9th of August, which was issued in Celine. At least that's what it says on the top. Is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, sometimes in the heading it said Gracac, other times it said Seline. Now, since in Seline the communication was more secure, whether we had to go to Seline or Gracac at that point in time I really can't remember, but Seline, anyway, was secure communication, and in Gracac we came across communications that had been cut off, and we needed two or three days to establish fixed communication lines, and during that time we used telephones with the help of radio devices and not wire connections, which were not secure. So maybe people went to Seline for a secure line in order to convey a document of this kind. So I really don't remember where we sent this particular document out from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you recall, how long were you still capable of using Seline as an additional back-up for communications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For about five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pavlovic. Let's move on to the appearance of Mr. Jarnjak. You mentioned him a couple of times. In your witness statement, you state in the last sentence that: "The minister of the interior, Mr. Jarnjak, came to Gracac and held a meeting with members of the staff and officially opened the newly established Gracac police station, because the conditions had been created for regular police members to maintain public law and order." Now, that was, I understand, on the 5th of August, in the evening, that Mr. Jarnjak came. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. Mr. Jarnjak, before that, came to a place called Lovinac where we opened a police station in the manner in which I have described. We put up a plaque saying "Police Station" on a destroyed building, on the only chimney that remained standing on that building, and after that Mr. Jarnjak set out towards Gracac. We greeted him there, and the staff meeting was held in the hallway of the Municipal Court where all the commanders were rallied together and the minister of the interior, Mr. Jarnjak, arrived. He greeted each of the members and congratulated us on a successful operation. After that, Mr. Jarnjak left and went to the former police station, the police station that wasn't destroyed during the war or during the liberation operation, and he open the police station once again of the Republic of Croatia there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But that wasn't an easy transition between the military and the civilian authorities. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, well, these police echelons took over their assignments. Whether it was an easy or difficult task I can't really say. I wasn't informed of that, because the person in charge was the assistant minister, Mr. Moric, and the chief of the sector, Mr. Franjo Djurica who then dealt with those affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So are you saying that you can't really state with any degree of certainty that the conditions had been created for regular police members to maintain public law and order? That's not something that you would be familiar with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I was at the Special Police headquarters all the time after all, and we were advancing towards the border of the Republic of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, towards Gornji Vakuf. So I really don't know whether the situation was difficult or not, whether it was difficult to set up regular police affairs, but I do know that in that area there were no more enemy forces to any great degree, and there was no reason why regular police business shouldn't be started.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This is, Mr. President, P614.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's a report, an analysis of the preparation of Operation Storm, dated 26th of November, 2001. And I'd like to show you in English a passage on page 18. And in Croatian, that's for you, Mr. Pavlovic, page 22. And here on the heeding, first we have "good experiences," discusses communications. That's your area. And then we have in the middle of the English page "Negative experiences and shortcomings." And the last paragraph under negative experiences reads as follows: "After some places had been liberated (Gracac, Bruvno, Donji Lapac) major problems arose as regards organising life and accommodation for people in them, since we had not established contact with the civilian organs of authorities in those areas in good time." Were you aware of those major problems in liaising with the civilian organs of authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, I wasn't. I didn't know that there were such problems. I wasn't an immediate participant in all this. But I do remember that already on the second day, so if we were in Gracac one day then on the second day representatives of the civilian authorities turned up, the person in charge for Gracac, and representatives of civilian protection. They came to our headquarters, and we talked to them about taking on the civilian affairs and seeing that everything ran smoothing in Gracac. As for the other towns, I have no detailed information about them. All I do know is that we had certain difficulties in certain areas, such as Donji Lapac, where we established a police station with very few means of communication, because we weren't able to set up the telephone lines with that particular police station. All that was used was radio communication in that area, so that when something needed to be conveyed, a written message or a conversation with someone or whatever, they either had to go to Gracac or they had to drive off to some higher elevation in order to establish radio communication with the particular police station they wanted to reach. So there were difficulties in respect of securing communication, electricity in the area, things like that. We used generators, as I've already said, quite a bit, so there were difficulties of that nature, but that was no reason for the tasks of the civilian authorities to be set up within those restricted conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But going back to the quote in this document, you were not aware, I think you said that, of these problems, major problems, regards organising life and accommodation because contact wasn't established in good time between the relevant authorities. That's -- you're saying you're not aware of any of these problems?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. Prosecutor. I didn't know of all the problems that existed surrounding the establishment of civilian -- the civilian authorities. I wasn't informed of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pavlovic. Let's move into the time you entered Gracac, and you described yesterday the entry of the Special Police. Now, I'm interested in your personally. When did you personally enter Gracac, if you recall, in terms of time but also in relation to the first combat, or whatever you want to call them, the first units or members of units of the Special Police that entered Gracac? How far behind them were you, or were you with the first ones to enter Gracac on the 5th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, no, I wasn't among the first to enter Gracac. In the meantime, when I left Seline I went to Sveti Rok to Lovinac where I stayed briefly until a police station had been officially opened, and after that I went towards Sveti Rok and across Ricice village towards Gracac. I would say that I spent two or three hours on my journey and that I arrived two or three hours after the first people who entered Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pavlovic. Now, you were asked yesterday about these so-called abandoned vehicles. Now you said on page 25254, and I quote you: "Pursuant to the order all vehicles and agriculture machinery should be taken to a collection point which had been predetermined." Who's order was that to take all these vehicles to a collection point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't remember who issued that order or those instructions, but I know that it was the civilian protection that was in charge of that kind of thing and designated the various collection points. I remember that there was talk at headquarters in Gracac, discussions with the commanders, that -- well, I'm not sure whether from General Markac or Mr. Sacic, I think it was General Markac. We heard that all vehicles, transportation vehicles and agricultural machinery should be handed over at collection points of that kind and that they should be deposited there until they decided what was to be done with -- with them. But let me tell you, it was a very small number of vehicles, and they were either out of order, technically, or had no fuel, and basically they were old vehicles such as the Stojadin, Lada, the caravan-type vehicle. We didn't find any luxury cars there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall when the order was -- or these instructions were given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember when exactly, Mr. Prosecutor, but I think it was on that same evening of the 5th when we were in Gracac. I think we mentioned that these should be removed because some of these vehicles were left on the road and obstructed communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And to whom was the order addressed? You mentioned civilian protection. Was it addressed to civilian protection or to somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The order was given to the commanders of the special units, and for them to pass the order on to their units, telling them that such vehicles and machinery should be handed over to the civilian protection people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where was the collection point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: These civilian protection people, when did they arrive, or were they in Gracac already when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their representatives, as I've already said, Mr. Prosecutor, arrived on the 6th in Gracac, but I don't remember when their units actually followed them into Gracac, because at that time I was already going towards Donji Lapac and Boricevci.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know how they looked like, these civilian protection people? Did they have uniforms? Were they in civilian outfits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The civilian protection had its own working uniforms, and they had insignia designating them as being members of the civilian protection force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were similar orders or instructions given in relation to these vehicles in relation to other towns or villages, as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same order applied wherever we moved around, that all the vehicles should be removed from the roads and left at the appropriate locations so that they could be collected up and then later on they would decide what to do with that property. Now, according to regulations of the Republic of Croatia, you cannot register a vehicle without the necessary papers proving purchase or whatever, and so we were told that vehicles couldn't be taken into a unit either because it wouldn't be possible to register them. And I know that we couldn't register a vehicle of that kind, and then the suggestion made was that no such vehicle should be taken into any units, but they should be left and collected up by the civilian authorities in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Kuzmanovic made reference to photos before the Trial Chamber, and I think he mentioned jump-starting a vehicle. Let me show you one of these photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is P324. And I'd like to go to the second of the photos. The first one is somebody loading an item onto a truck, and the second one is this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, first of all, Mr. Pavlovic, have you seen this photograph before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I haven't, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise the soldier, uniformed person, on this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But can you confirm that he's a member of the Special Police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, judging by the insignia on his left arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I can tell you that this picture, photograph, was taken on the 8th of August in Gracac. Were you in Gracac on the 8th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 8th of August, in the afternoon, I was at a meeting in Boricevci where enemy artillery, that is to say tanks, fired at us, and I remember that I was on that day at the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you are not in a position to tell the Trial Chamber what the motivation of this soldier could be in jump-starting this car.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. There could be a number of reasons, that he received an order to remove it, and as most probably there were no keys available he tried to start in a way that was possible. And as we can see, and as I said, the car is I believe a Lada or something similar, so it's not a luxury car. It was left there either because it was in disrepair or because there were no papers for it, but I cannot see from the photo what could be the reason for the person doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you agree with me that it does not appear that this car was in any way interfering, you know, with communications or with traffic? It looks like it's on a parking lot or whatever just in front of a house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you are supposing now, just as I can suppose. I don't know what was the reason why he was doing this. Maybe he had received an order that this car should be removed to the dump.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what -- why would that be the job of the elite unit Special Police to remove cars like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it is hard for me to say what member this was, whether he was the member of the relevant police administration which remained in the area after the 8th of August or some other unit. I cannot comment on what was -- what exactly was happening there just on the basis of this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: If we could move to the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, could I seek some clarification. These places where these vehicles had to be taken, who predetermined where these places were? Who decided where -- where these vehicles had to be taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not know that, but I suppose that the civilian protection had its plan about the places where the vehicles would be taken and then agreed on these places with the regular police. As far as I can remember, in Gracac it was a farm behind the school, but I'm not certain, and I cannot guarantee that because I wasn't interested in that part of our work. I wasn't involved in that, so I didn't really pay much attention to such issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How would -- how would your people know where to take them? Civilian authority was already there to determine where these vehicles had to be taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I said, I was the assistant commander for operative duties, and those under my command who were in the area were on the move all the time. They did not stay behind, and they could not receive such tasks to move or remove abandoned vehicles from the roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But isn't it true that your testimony yesterday said that that's what you had to do and that they had to be taken to predetermined places? Now you're telling us more or less that you were -- that this was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, but I didn't say that I had to do that or my people but that this was one of the task of the Special Police members, that they should remove certain vehicles from the road so that they would not obstruct the advance and passing of our units and our transportation equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said: "Those under my commander who were in the area, who were on the move all the time, they did not stay behind, and they could not receive such tasks to move or removed abandoned vehicles from the road." Yesterday you said that that's what you had to do in order to -- to avoid that communications would be -- would be obstructed. And then you told us and, well, where they had to be taken, that it was predetermined, and it now seems that you're not fully familiar with -- and you said -- earlier I asked where it was and you said, "I don't know." A minute later you said, "I think it was a farm behind a school." What made you believe that it was a farm behind a school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a lot of time has passed since then. Sometimes I see some images in my recollection when I try to prove the truth, but I said that I could not say with certainty. It seems to me that I remember that it could have been there, but at the same time I cannot really assert that that was the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is that image a place that you've seen cars there, or is that image anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the images of such cars, because I remember that in several spots we had to circle such vehicles, because sometimes they obstructed more than half of the road. And I remember that the bonnets were sometimes up, and I just have in my mind these images of those abandoned vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but your images came up upon a question of where they had to be placed. I was talking about the farm behind the school, and then you say sometimes images come up. Now that seems to be a different image from the image you are telling us about now which is in line with your earlier testimony, that they had to be removed, but again, my question was focused on the predetermined place where they had to be taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I talked about these vehicles and when they were removed, I was talking about the very short time after the operation only, but as we spent more time in Gracac over this longer period, the information was collected, that is to say, what I learned about this. So I didn't know on the first or the second day where such a place would be or even that it existed, but then later on I was informed about that, and then I tried to explain the procedure that was conducted on these later days. I did not expressly say that this took place immediately on the 5th or 6th of August of that year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did you then at that later stage see these places where these cars were deposited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. In general, I passed most of my time either at the staff or I had to tour certain areas. I didn't walk around much, but during the conversation at the headquarters with commanders I would learn some of these details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Talking about the procedures, did you at that time learn who predetermined the places where these cars had to be deposited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but I said that I believe that civilian protection units determined these places in agreement with regular police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Last question talking about images. When you were interviewed, was the photo which is now on your screen, was that shown to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Waespi. It's time for the break. We'll have a break, and we will resume -- perhaps I should say you can resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having urged the parties to conclude today, if possible, you will understand that it was really an urgent matter which kept me for such a long time out of this courtroom. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think I'll be done within half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, you mentioned in your witness statement at paragraph 10 that you were with General Markac during most of Operation Storm, attended all the meetings before significant operative actions and actions to search the terrain. Now, were you aware that General Markac met with the chiefs of the police administrations and police coordinators to try and resolve some of the problems that cropped up in the aftermath of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't remember such details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's not something General Markac would have briefed you during the evening meetings of the command staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. As far as I remember, this was not mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Markac [sic]. Let's go to Donji Lapac, the entry of the Special Police and yourself. When did you enter yourself? And again I mean you personally. When did you enter Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, as far as I remember, it was sometime around 15 or 1530 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's on the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember how far behind the first elements of the Special Police you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand your question exactly, Mr. Prosecutor, but I will try to explain. In front of us the infantry advanced, and we were in a convoy of vehicles that was continuing its movement immediately after them. So after the infantry, the convoy of vehicles advanced behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in your witness statement you mention in paragraph 17, the second sentence, that in Donji Lapac you found out that the Serbs had torched some buildings in the centre of town. Now, how did you find out that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, on arrival to the centre of the town where the police station was, I noticed that the police station was hit by a shell directly and that the building behind it was on fire, as was another building for which I heard was the building of the hotel. I do not remember, but somebody told me that the Serbs had torched one of these buildings during their withdrawal. I don't who, but I remember that someone on the spot told me that. I could not ascertain whether that was the truth or not, but this is why I said in my statement that I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. You testified yesterday that the majority of the Special Police then went on towards Boricevci and other elements stayed behind, and the elements that stayed behind were logistics, some of your communications elements, and Commander Janic and his unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I left Lapac, members of the Communications Unit remained there, as well as members of logistics and Janic with some of his soldiers. And then later on in the communications that I listened to, because I was listening to communication all the time, anything that I could reach and anything that I could hear, I heard that he received an order to remove his units from the town to border areas, that he should take a position, and that his unit should have some rest outside of the town of Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is that what you referred to yesterday as being on holiday in -- in Donji Lapac? At least the interpretation we received yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. They were not involved in further activities in the direction of the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is to say Kulen Vakuf, but they were having some rest. It was not holiday, it was a short rest, because for two or two and a half or three days we were practically on the move all the time. It was just a deserved rest so that they would gather some strength for further activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The comment of yesterday was at page 25266: "Units of the Special Police, you were on holiday in Lapac." That's what you just referred to a second ago?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that what she said yesterday she added by saying on furlough as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not on holiday. It was just a confusion. I don't think the document says that anywhere. It was only on the 8th that we started pulling out the units and sending them to base for real rest. So it was beginning on the 8th that the units were being pulled out of combat activities. That is the 8th of August that I have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you continue in your witness statement to say that you spent a short time with General Markac in Donji Lapac. How long did you stay in Donji Lapac on that afternoon of the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I think that I stayed for about two hours in Donji Lapac, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then you left the city and came back the next day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. The next day I returned, because the establishment of the police station or regular police began, so I went there for an agreement about the duties that had to be discharged so that at least the radio communications would start functioning in the area and that we could agree on the way in which we would secure further communication so that the police station could begin to operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in terms of exact timing, do you recall when you left Donji Lapac on the 7th? I quote from your transcript of yesterday. That's 25262 where you say: "I myself, towards afternoon, I can't remember the exact time, but between 2.00 and 3.00 p.m., I was still in the area and that's when the shelling started from -- coming from an unknown direction or, rather, from unknown units, and so I left Lapac immediately after that." So approximately when did you leave Lapac that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In terms of time, Mr. Prosecutor, I cannot say exactly how long it took, but I think it could have been around 17 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you were not around then when members of the 118th Home Guard Regiment and the 9th Guards Brigade and maybe other units entered Donji Lapac at around 7.00 or 7.30 on the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, I did not see when they entered Donji Lapac, but by monitoring the communications system, I simply learned that they had entered Donji Lapac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you also don't know what happened that night, the night of the 7th and 8th of August in Donji Lapac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. I didn't see myself what happened, but by listening to radio communications I heard what was happening in the area, because Commander Janic called several times on the radio communications system and reported about what was happening and what was the scope of destruction in the area after the entry of the 118th Home Guard Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you have no personal knowledge from your own observations on who would have set fire on the houses, who the perpetrators would be, and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, I did not see any of that personally, and therefore I cannot assert something that I did not see. I know what I heard, but I didn't see for myself who torched the houses, nor was I present in Donji Lapac at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pavlovic, for answering these questions. I don't have any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just have two questions in redirect. First -- well, two topics. The first if we could please pull up D504.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, and this concerns Minister Jarnjak's appearance at Gracac on August 5 of 1995. D504 is a transcript and a short video of that event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 507. I apologise. D507. My error. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The transcript here from the reporter in this HTV video-clip shows that -- it states the reporter speaking: "This morning at around 11.00 special units of the Ministry of the Interior entered Gracac. The Minister of the Interior Ivan Jarnjak visited his boys." Do you recall this visit at -- being after 11.00 on August 5th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Minister Jarnjak did not come there at 11.00. This is wrongly written, Counsel. The minister got there in the afternoon, and he came to visit us at the Municipal Court in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe you missed -- maybe my question wasn't stated clearly or it was misinterpreted. The transcript here of this video clip says: "This morning at around 11.00 the special units of the Ministry of the Interior entered Gracac." My question to you was: Minister Jarnjak then came into Gracac after 11.00, meaning after the special forces arrived; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel. He got there in the afternoon, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Why don't we play the clip. It's only a few seconds long.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] This morning at around 11.00 the special units of the Ministry of the Interior entered Gracac. The minister of the interior, Ivan Jarnjak, visited his boys. The chief of the Zadar-Knin police administration, Ivica Setina, set up a sign at the police station building with the words: 'Police Administration Knin, Police Station Gracac.' "There you go, gentlemen. Now let Rukavina come. "It's not hanging right. Fix it a little bit. "Now come here, first the chief. "This is the first police station in the newly liberated area. Good luck. So it be. "The deputy commander, as the commander has not yet arrived, good luck to you. Keep the law and order as it has always been in Croatia, according to the law and order. Secure the law and order, protect the property and everything else. Good luck and take care."

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, there's no time noted on this video, but you can see it's during the daylight hours that this occurred; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: The other question or topic area that I wanted to discuss with you concerned your testimony at page 24, lines 3 through 5, regarding civilians and what the Special Police was requested to do of them. I just want you to tell the Chamber that with respect to civilians, was what the Special Police was doing when they encountered civilians something that they did to protect them or was it something they did to try to remove them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Special Police did not have the task to take care of civilians, but during briefings and in the analysis before operation we were told that the civilians should be sent to the relevant regular police, that they had to report themselves to it, and then the further procedure was taken up by the regular police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: One final question with respect to the removal of vehicles. The Special Police had technical expertise in terms of encountering not just in vehicles but in other places booby-traps, mines. Is that a reason for the Special Police to be involved in certain instances in checking out vehicles and buildings? I'll repeat the question. Please wait a second, because part of my question wasn't translated into Croatian. I'll read the question exactly again as it stands. "The Special Police had technical expertise in terms of encountering not just in vehicles but in other places booby-traps, mines. Is that a reason for the Special Police to be involved in certain instances in checking out vehicles and buildings?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give a reason as to why Special Police would be involved in removal of vehicles and/or checking out buildings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Defence Counsel. During the war between 1991 and 1995, Special Police had gained a lot of knowledge, and it was specialised in securing certain areas. So their main task was to fight against terrorism. That was their main task within the Ministry of the Interior, and as such they were qualified to execute a number of jobs. They had lots of knowledge, and how they put it, there were many areas in which they had to work. One of their duties was the de-mining of liberated territories, entering certain facilities for which we could suppose that they might be mined, as well as vehicles and other abandoned items. These could be booby-traps, and therefore they inspected such facilities and vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether that particular day in Medak a member of the Special Police was wounded as a result of something similar to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Defence Counsel. I'm not certain if it was in the village of Medak itself, but I know that at a check-point on the way to Gospic there was a mine hanging, that is to say a hand grenade, and when the ramp was lifted, the ramp on the road, they wanted to remove it, and then this hand grenade exploded and several of them were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuzmanovic. Any further questions, Mr. Kehoe? Mr. Kay? No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, you talked about how you experienced the high morale of Mr. Markac. Could you imagine Mr. Markac falsely accusing the opposite forces of having launched a sabotage attack as a pretext for his own -- for his own military activity, that is, just to create a provocative action which had not taken place in order to justify his own military behaviour? Could you imagine in your assessment of the morale of Mr. Markac such a thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Mr. Markac, or General Markac, is first and foremost a policeman at heart. That is how he was brought up. And the military activities were imposed upon us, and we had the physical and psychological ability. We were trained to have the ability to deal with difficult situations.
