We were up there on Mount Velebit. We were there three years. So that would be the only reason why we went into military action. But we never looked for a conflict, nor did we provoke a conflict, nor can I imagine that General Markac would ever do that in order -- as a pretext for his own military actions. That was not in his nature. It wasn't in our nature or a single member of General Markac's staff. We were first and foremost policemen and only secondly soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If he would have said words coming close to what I described at a meeting, would you be surprised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to come back briefly to your -- to the other matter I raised before the break, that is about the cars. I would like to know exactly from you what you observed personally. From your testimony, I took it that you saw vehicles obstructing part of the road, some with their hoods open. Could you tell us what else you personally observed from removal of cars, whether cars in this position or cars anywhere else? Could you tell us what you personally observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure I understood which area you meant. Only the Gracac area or while Operation Storm was going on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about -- I'm asking you this question in the context of your earlier testimony, you remember that cars were to be taken somewhere. You told us about cars that had to be removed because they were on the road and they were obstructing communication. That's the context in which I ask you this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was like this: I personally saw several vehicles, not many, five or six perhaps, in Gracac, at the entrance to Donji Lapac that were obstructing the road itself. Now, I have quite a bit of information about that, because I listened to the radio communications and I learned many things. I heard about them but I didn't see them myself, except while I was driving along the road myself I saw these vehicles. But all the other activities that took place, both with respect to issuing orders that certain vehicles be removed and orders to search certain vehicles which might have been placed there on purpose as sabotage, I heard all that through the communication system. And I mentioned them here because I wanted to show you, Your Honours, and both parties what the situation was like and that we wanted to deal with everything that we came across in certain locations and well -- we received instructions or when I heard about instructions during conversations at meetings or through the communications network, because I listened to the Special Police communications and the regular police communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Quite simple, did you learn in this way that these cars had to be removed, that orders were given?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's how I learnt about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Who would then give such an order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times I heard General Markac telling the commanders that the vehicles and agricultural machinery should be removed and taken to certain locations and that they were given the task of doing that and seeing that the vehicles were handed over as soon as possible and that they were not to be used for Special Police purposes, if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But from -- I understand from your testimony that they were used for Special Police purposes sometimes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, while we were in the area. We had instructions not to drive the vehicles away from the area because they wouldn't be able to be registered nor used for daily duties of special units in their original bases. So those vehicles were only used in the area while we were in Sector South.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, were instructions -- did you learn about instructions through radio as well that such limited use of cars just within the area was accepted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Your Honour, that that was only through radio communication. I think it was discussed at staff meetings which took place every day in the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you personally observe the use of those vehicles for local Special Police purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour I did not. I've already said that throughout that time I was at headquarters when I was in those bases, so that I wasn't out in the open much to see those vehicles being used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you learn about it if you didn't see it yourself? What was the information you received on the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was information coming in from time to time that the Special Police forces were driving vehicles that weren't registered, and there was the danger of them entering into an area where they would not be recognised and then our forces could target them. So the recommendation was that that -- those vehicles should be used as little as possible, and if they were used, then these units using them would place their name on the car. I remember that there were a couple of cars like that where the unit's name was written up on them, but the recommendation was that the vehicles should be handed over to the civilian protection as soon as possible and that there was no need to use them too often.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you would see these cars driving around with the names of units on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I just saw on the photograph that was shown. I saw that there was writing on that, and I saw that the name "Delta" was written up on the vehicle, which was a Special Police Unit. There was one by that name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I earlier asked you whether you had seen this photograph during your interview. Did you see that photograph at any time, at any place before you came to court yesterday or today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I just saw it a while ago when you showed it to me -- or, rather, when the Prosecutor showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Any further questions triggered by the questions by the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pavlovic, this then concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming the long way to The Hague and for answering all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And as I said before, I would give an opportunity to raise some procedural issues later today. And I do understand, Mr. Misetic, that the Gotovina Defence would like to bar table or to seek admission as a bar table exhibit a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is 65 ter number 1643. This is a leaflet discussed at -- in Mr. Theunens's report, P113, part 2, pages 199 to 200. We would ask that it be moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You'll understand that it does not immediately ring a bell what at that page Mr. Theunens said. Could you briefly describe the leaflet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could pull it up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so that we know what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was some discussion with Mr. Granic last week from the Bench about leaflets, I believe. If I'm not mistaken, it was Mr. Granic. It was -- part of the Brioni transcript was read back to Mr. Granic, and it is the position of the Gotovina Defence that the leaflet discussed at Brioni is the leaflet which we now have on the screen. The Prosecution may take a different position, but nevertheless given that we had been content with simply leaving into -- in Mr. Theunens's report, but given that one leaflet has already been offered into evidence by the Prosecution, we believe that this leaflet should have been a separate exhibit and get its own number for reasons that I think later on will be relevant in terms of arguing the leaflet discussed at Brioni and which one was discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi, Mr. Carrier, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can we have some more information about the source of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's a Prosecution document, and it's cited by Mr. Theunens in his report, so I would just direct Mr. Waespi to Mr. Theunens's report on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'll have to look into that and report back, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, from our position it is in evidence already. It's just a question of whether we can have it marked as a separate exhibit since Mr. Theunens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Relied upon it, you would say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it should and reason that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Chamber couldn't ignore --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes and cited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, would you agree with that if Mr. Theunens cites this document that there's no way out unless you would withdraw the report of Mr. Theunens in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No. I agree with you. I just need to see Theunens's report, whether it corresponds. I'm not doubting it. I just need some time to look into it, but I agree with the reasoning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Usually we ask for joint filing of bar table documents, but I think that all the purposes that are served by that procedure are served by now, that is the relevance has been explained, specific portions we have to pay attention to is for a one-page document is not really something. There's one issue which is about the handwriting on it -- on the document. Any explanation for that, because I do not know what was there before. Something is stricken out and now says "Obrovac and Benkovac" and there must have been something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, this is a document we received from the Prosecution, and it's -- this is the document, I believe, cited by Mr. Theunens in his report. So it is offered the way it was received by us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which doesn't take away that there may be questions about it. If any further explanation for that striking out and handwriting could be provided, the Chamber would appreciate that. Mr. Registrar, this document would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that, will become Exhibit D1832.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Then there was apparently another translation issue which -- yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could cover that. I would like to turn back to the document D420, which was discussed during the testimony of Mr. Pejkovic. In the meantime, we obtained two missing pages in the Croatian version of that document, and we would like to load them into the version -- or into the Croatian version of the document so that this version could be totally completed, not with the missing two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And we had a conversation with Mr. Registrar, and I think that could be provided quite easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there were two issues, if I'm -- if my recollection serves me well. The first were the two missing pages. The other one was whether the two originals, one original in English, one original in B/C/S, whether there was any substantial difference between the content of it, and I think, Mr. Mikulicic, but correct me when I'm wrong, that we invited the Markac Defence to specifically compare the two pages that were missing, but apart from that, also to have a more general look at the document to see whether these two originals could be considered of, if not the full hundred per cent, at least the 99 per cent same content, apart from issues of time periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Our position is like this: We checked the document, although I could not say with a hundred per cent certainty, but as it turns to our position, both documents are original version and there is no great discrepancies between those two versions. But what I would suggest is that we wait a little while to hear from the Prosecution side whether their checking had accomplished some other results, and afterwards we could easily join together and inform the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. It was a document that was tendered by Mr. Kuzmanovic during Mr. Galbraith's testimony. It's been used again extensively now by the Markac Defence during Mr. Pejkovic's testimony. I think just to close the issue it would be better if the Markac Defence submitted the Croatian version for translation so that there's one version. Presumably they didn't write two separate documents at the same time. They wrote a Croatian version of the document. I think that's apparent. So I think that there should be corresponding translation of that document. That should be relied on. And then to invite the Prosecution to do that work for the Markac Defence, the Prosecution submits it's not our duty to do that. It's the person tendering the document, putting it into evidence, that should ensure that there's a proper translation. So I would ask that the Markac Defence take that on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Very practically, again how many pages were there, approximately, the whole of document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: It was roughly 50 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fifty in the English. Well, let's say -- I think there were something like 33 in the Croatian, but I'm not certain about that. Have you considered how much time that takes from CLSS to have that translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: I have given that. I was also asked to try to do that during the course of the day in the middle of the witness. I know how difficult it would be to compare, so I understand with direct knowledge how difficult it would be. That's why I think it would be better just to have one document. And so for our translators to sit down and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm just thinking in terms of resources. I'm a very practical person in that respect. It will take days and days to have this all translated, whereas whether there's a real pressing need is not yet explored. One way of exploring would be, and I'm just giving this as a suggestion, you're sitting in a room, Defence and Prosecution, or someone at least who can read the language, reads out one paragraph loud in the one version, and then the same paragraph is read in the other version. If these two persons do understand the other language as well, and it must be possible to find bilingual persons in both teams, then they could see whether there's any substantial difference in the language used. Let's not forget that this is not an order to attack, or this is not a -- this is a document which explains years after the events what apparently was done by the government, what the plans were, how they -- I mean, it's -- it's -- I wouldn't say marginal, but it's certainly not at the core of the case. Now, I can imagine that it would take you -- two persons, a couple of hours. Six hours, seven hours, eight hours for the two persons together. Then you would have established whether there really is a need to have 50 pages translated, which might take days and days and days of our resources. I do not know exactly what it is, but I think it's six or eight pages a day, which would keep someone busy for six or seven days. We have to be, and this has got nothing to do with -- it's just a management issue, and I would like you and the Defence to consider to do this exploration first before the Chamber will finally decide on whether or not the Markac Defence will be instructed to provide a new translation. Is that a matter you'd be willing to consider?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: By all means, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes. I'll ask somebody on our team to meet and spend the time with someone from the Markac Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You look as if you're quite unhappy with it. That's a read from your face.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: No, no. I'm just -- just trying to be as practical as possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's appreciated. Then if there still is a need to have a full translation, the Chamber will hear from you first of all, Mr. Carrier, because it would be that you're not satisfied with the results. Any other matter? If not, then -- let me just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, Mr. Registrar drew my attention to the fact that I had not yet responded to the new uploaded two pages, but I think it was already implied in my earlier instructions that they should be uploaded so that at least not the one reading has two pages less to read than the other one. So therefore, please may the two pages be included in the uploaded Croatian version of this document. Tomorrow it's a UN holiday. We have no further witnesses for today. Therefore, we -- we adjourn and resume on Monday, the 30th of November, 9.00 in the morning in Courtroom III.
